statement: 2. Collusion-Resistant CPRFs for predicated range from LWE. We generalize our main CPRF construction to support predicated range constraints (i.e., range checking on function output). Each constraint predicate CC[f, y, z] is associated with a ‘compute’ function f and an output range [y, z], where an input x satisfies the predicate if f (x) ∈ [y, z]. We prove our CPRF for predicated range satisfies collusion-resistant constrained pseudorandomness as long as the ranges are pairwise disjoint. We leave it as an interesting open question to prove constraint privacy for this constraint class.

We leave it as an interesting open question to prove constraint privacy for this constraint class. 3. 2-Sided Predicate Encryption. As a direct application of our CPRFs, we construct a collusion-resistant 2-sided (or strongly attribute-hiding) predicate encryption (PE) scheme [BW07, KSW08, GKW17a] for compute-&-compare predicates under standard LWE. Our encryption system is a symmetric-key scheme and also satisfies predicate privacy (i.e., decryption keys hide the predicate). Prior to this work, 2-sided PE could only be built for inner-product predicates [BW07, KSW08], or by invoking obfuscation and related primitives [GGH+ 13b, SW14, ABSV15]. Key-Homomorphism: an added benefit. Our CPRF constructions also satisfy (almost-)key-homomorphic property w.r.t. the master key as well as constrained keys [BLMR13, BFP+ 15, CVW+ 18a, GQWW19]. Briefly, (almost-)key-homomorphism states that FK1 (x) + FK2 (x) ≈ FK1 +K2 (x), where K1 , K2 are two master keys or two constrained keys for the same predicate. The key-homomorphism property has proven to be extremely valuable for a variety for applications [BLMR13, BFP+ 15, CVW+ 18a, GQWW19] and, to the best of our knowledge, we did not have any collusion-resistant key-homomorphic CPRF for any predicate other than prefix-fixing predicates from standard assumptions.

This restriction can be removed in the random oracle model by the standard output-hashing transformation. The variant keeps the same constrained keys and the same algebraic evaluation procedure, but replaces the final output zx by H(zx ). For an admissible challenge input x⋆ , the underlying value zx⋆ remains hidden from the adversary by the security of the base construction. Thus, except with negligible probability, the adversary never queries zx⋆ to the random oracle. Conditioned on this event, H(zx⋆ ) is a fresh random string, and the simulator may program this value as the challenge output. At a high level, our plan is to combine our base CPRF construction with the prefixfixing CRPF based on GGM [GGM86] PRFs. Essentially, our idea is to ensure that the user of the constrained keys can do partial evaluation over the tree instead of only given the leaf vectors. More concretely, given sT · Ay + noise as part of the constrained secret key, the user can locally approximate the value of sT · Ay|y′ for any y ′ . To achieve this, rather than adopting the framework of Banerjee-Peikert [BP14], we instead follow the approach of Boneh et al. [BLMR13]. The issue with [BP14] is that it computes Ay using a binary tree structure rather than sequentially. While it improves concrete efficiency, it is unclear whether the prefix-fixing ideas could be applied there. On the other hand, evaluation in [BLMR13] proceeds sequentially. statement: We highlight that although our collusion-resistant CPRF construction naturally extends our compute-&-compare CPRF scheme, we are unable to generalize it to prove (full) constraint hiding. The issue is that, if we rely on a similar homomorphic-encryption-based constraint hiding template, evaluating f (x) requires explicitly using f to ‘select’ the partial key corresponding to a prefix of f (x). Thus, the evaluator needs some information about f (x) (which is just the maximum length of the matching prefix as per above decomposition) in order to correctly evaluate the PRF. However, we note that if an evaluator gets this additional information, then we can indeed prove constraint hiding for predicated range circuits. We believe such a weaker notion of constraint hiding might be useful for certain applications, and we leave the problem of constraint hiding for predicated range circuits as an interesting open problem.

By combining the above with the fact that any range constraint (even of exponential size) can be decomposed into polynomially many prefix checks (using the power-of-two trick), we can give out constrained keys for arbitrary range predicates efficiently. To illustrate this, consider the following simple example: let [y, z] be the desired range, where y = 0010 and z = 1011. The key-constraining algorithm will assign partial keys corresponding to 0012, 0122, and 1022, where 2 denotes a wildcard position. Using this, the constraining algorithm can generate compute-&-compare -style constrained keys for differing length targets. We believe such a weaker notion of constraint hiding might be useful for certain applications, and we leave the problem of constraint hiding for predicated range circuits as an interesting open problem. 2.4 Applications to 2-Sided Predicate Encryption We explore the implications of our construction to 2-sided predicate encryption (PE), contrasting it with the more common 1-sided variant. In a standard PE scheme [BW07, KSW08], a secret key skf enables the decryption of a ciphertext associated with attribute x if and only if f (x) = 1. In the 1-sided setting, attribute-hiding is required only when f (x) = 0. In the 2-sided setting, x must remain computationally hidden even from a user who possesses a key that successfully decrypts the ciphertext (i.e., when f (x) = 1). Achieving 2-sided security for general predicates is notoriously difficult, as it is essentially equivalent to collusion-resistant Functional Encryption [SW05, BW07, KSW08, BSW11]. 12

context: 3. 1-Sided Encryption: Encrypts m using a 1-sided PE scheme under the augmented attribute (ctx , τ ). To create a secret key, we first sample a constrained PRF key for a compute-&-compare predicate (f, y) that decrypts ctx and checks if f (Dec(k, ctx )) = y. Next, we sample a 1-sided PE key that checks if the CPRF evaluation (using the above constrain key) on the ciphertext matches the tag τ . Because the message is “shielded” by the CPRF tag, an adversary learns only the bit representing the success of the evaluation, leaving x hidden even upon successful decryption. Our scheme only works in the symmetric-key setting as the encryptor needs to evaluate the CPRF for obtaining the ‘tag’ in the ciphertext. We leave it as an exciting open problem to generalize our construction to the public-key setting. 2.5 Discussion and Future Directions Boosting to Impure Classes. A natural question is whether CPRFs for purified constraints can serve as a mechanism to bootstrap to more expressive, “impure” classes. While a jump to general circuits is likely precluded by some complexity theoretic lower bounds, we provide partial positive results for “weakly impure” constraints in Section 11. We define a circuit class C as weakly impure if any C ∈ C can be expressed as a sum of poly(λ) purified circuits C1 , . . . , Ck from a purified class C ′ . To issue a key for C ∈ C, the authority generates k independent CPRF keys for the constituent purified circuits. This allows us to handle predicates with bounded overlaps. For example, consider a range-based class where two keys might overlap on a small, fixed-length interval. By “purifying” these overlaps during the key-generation phase (i.e., treating the intersection as its own disjoint sub-predicate) we can extend the utility of our construction to non-disjoint settings.

Open Question: Towards Arbitrary Purified Constraints. Our work leaves open the challenge of designing CPRFs for arbitrary purified circuit classes. Specifically, can we construct collusion-resistant CPRFs for any poly-size constraints where the only guarantee is that their supports are disjoint? An affirmative answer from standard lattice assumptions would be a major breakthrough, as it would suggest that “zeroizing” attacks are the primary obstacles to collusion resistance. In Section 12, we provide a candidate CPRF for log-depth constraints which we conjecture to be secure 13 under purified corruption. We provide a proof under an extremely strong non-falsifiable lattice assumption, and pose the formal proof under a falsifiable lattice assumption (or cryptanalysis) of this candidate as an open problem.
